name: Object-Oriented Programming
author: Recurse
subject: programming
description: Model data with Python classes: __init__ and self, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, dunder methods and composition.

lesson.intro: Classes let you create your own types: data bundled with the behavior that belongs to it. This lesson covers objects, __init__ and self, class attributes, protecting an object's rules, inheritance, polymorphism, dunder methods and composition, which show up in every codebase and interview.
objectives: Define classes with __init__, attributes and methods, and explain self
Predict class attributes, instance attributes and shadowing
Protect an object's rules with validating methods and read-only properties
Use inheritance, super() and polymorphism, and composition for has-a relationships
Implement __str__, __repr__ and __eq__ so objects print and compare sensibly

sections.title: Why classes? Bundling data with behavior
sections.key: A class bundles data (attributes) with the behavior that belongs to it (methods); the class is the blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
sections.body:
A game has three players, each with a name, a score and items, handled by functions like `add_points(player, n)` that take a dict. It works until someone writes `player["scroe"] = 10`, or nobody can tell which functions are for players. The data and its code live apart.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

You have used objects all along: a string is an instance of `str`, and `"hi".upper()` calls one of its methods. `type(x)` names any value's class.

Reach for a class when values always travel together (a point's x and y), when there are rules to protect (a balance cannot go negative), or when several kinds of thing answer the same request differently. A function that turns input into output needs no class.

visual.title: One class, two instances
visual.caption: Each instance has its own attribute values and shares the class's methods.

visual.title: Vocabulary
visual.caption: Class names use `CapWords` (`ShoppingCart`); methods and attributes use `snake_case`.

sections.code:
class Player:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.score = 0

    def add_points(self, n):
        self.score += n

ana = Player("Ana")
bo = Player("Bo")
ana.add_points(10)
print(ana.score, bo.score)  # 10 0
print(type(ana).__name__)  # Player
sections.pitfall: Wrapping everything in classes. A function that takes input and returns output is often simpler. Use a class when data and the rules about it belong together.

check.question: After a = Account("Ana") and b = Account("Bo"), how many classes and instances are involved?
check.explanation: Account is defined once, and each call to Account(...) builds a separate instance from that one blueprint, each with its own attributes.

sections.title: Classes, instances, __init__ and self
sections.key: Calling `Dog("Rex", 3)` creates an object and runs `__init__` on it; inside every method, `self` is the object the method was called on.
sections.body:
`rex = Dog("Rex", 3)` does two things: Python creates a new, empty Dog, then calls `__init__`, the **initializer** (often called the constructor), to give it its starting attributes.

The first parameter of every method, named `self` by convention, is the object the method was called on:

[[visual]]

Store attributes with `self.name = value`. Without `self.`, a name inside a method is just a local variable that vanishes when the method returns. Read attributes with `rex.name` from outside, or `self.name` inside other methods.

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: What a method call means
visual.caption: That is how one method definition works for every dog.

visual.title: Rules to internalize
rows: Python passes the instance anyway: forget `self` and the call raises TypeError
Set every attribute in `__init__`, even as 0, None or `[]`
Readers see the object's full shape in one place
It configures the object; the call `Dog(...)` produces it
Each instance has its own attributes
`self.birthday()`; a method that ends with `return self` can be chained

sections.code:
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    def birthday(self):
        self.age += 1
        return self.age

rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
fido = Dog("Fido", 5)
print(rex.birthday())  # 4
print(fido.age)  # 5, fido is unaffected
sections.pitfall: Forgetting `self.` when storing or reading an attribute. `name = name` inside `__init__` only sets a local variable, and the object never gets a name.

activity.title: Add methods to a class
activity.prompt: Write deposit and withdraw as methods: each takes self and an amount and changes self.balance. Run it after each method to watch the error change.

props.code:
class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, owner):
        self.owner = owner
        self.balance = 0

    # Add deposit(amount) and withdraw(amount) methods here.


acct = BankAccount("Ana")
acct.deposit(100)
acct.withdraw(30)
print(acct.owner, acct.balance)
props.task: Add the two methods so the program prints exactly: Ana 70

check.question: When you call rex.birthday(), what is self inside the method?
check.explanation: Python passes the object before the dot as the first argument, so self is rex itself, not a copy. That's why self.age += 1 changes rex.age.

sections.title: Class attributes and instance attributes
sections.key: Python reads an attribute from the instance first and then the class, so a class attribute is shared by every instance until an instance attribute shadows it.
sections.body:
Every dog has its own name, but all dogs have four legs, and you might count how many dogs exist. An **instance attribute** is set on one object, usually in `__init__` with `self.x = ...`. A **class attribute** is assigned in the class body and shared by every instance.

[[visual]]

The classic bug is a mutable class attribute: `members = []` in the class body is one list shared by every instance, so appending through one object shows in all of them. Create per-object lists, dicts and sets in `__init__`.

Two decorators change what a method receives:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: The lookup rule in action
rows: `rex.legs`, when rex has no `legs` of its own
Creates an instance attribute on rex only, which **shadows** the class value; other dogs still see the class value
Changes the shared value for every instance that does not shadow it
Reads the class value, then writes a new instance attribute: the class counter never moves

items.title: @classmethod
points: Mostly for alternative constructors: `Temp.from_fahrenheit(212)` converts its input, then returns `cls(...)`

items.title: @staticmethod
points: Receives neither the instance nor the class
A plain function that belongs in the class logically

sections.pitfall: Putting a list or dict in the class body when each instance needs its own. Create it in `__init__` with `self.items = []`.

check.question: class Cat has the class attribute sound = "meow". You create a = Cat() and b = Cat(), then run a.sound = "purr". What is b.sound?
check.explanation: a.sound = "purr" creates an instance attribute on a only. b has no sound of its own, so the lookup falls through to the class and finds "meow".

sections.title: Encapsulation: guarding an object's rules
sections.key: An object should guard its own rules: change state only through methods that validate and raise errors, and expose read-only values with `@property`.
sections.body:
A balance should change only through deposits and withdrawals and never go below zero. If any code can write `acct.balance = -500`, that rule is only a hope. **Encapsulation** means an object controls access to its own state, so its rules (its **invariants**) always hold.

[[visual]]

Real protection comes from methods. `deposit()` and `withdraw()` check their input and `raise ValueError("amount must be positive")` when a rule would break, instead of quietly producing a broken object. Validate in `__init__` too.

A **property** (`@property`) exposes a value like a plain attribute while running code behind it. Without a setter it is read-only: `acct.balance = 50` raises AttributeError. Properties also suit computed values such as an area, which then never go stale.

visual.title: Python's privacy conventions
rows: Internal: do not touch from outside. Only a convention, but every Python developer and linter respects it
**Name mangling**: stored as `_ClassName__code`, so `s.__code` from outside raises AttributeError. Meant to avoid clashes in subclasses, not real privacy

sections.pitfall: Storing a value that should be computed, like an area stored next to its width and height. When one changes, the stored value goes stale; use a property instead.

activity.title: Fix a stale attribute with a property
activity.prompt: Run it: the area still says 12 after the width changed, because it was calculated once in __init__. Delete that line and add an area method decorated with @property that computes width times height each time it's read.

props.code:
class Rectangle:
    def __init__(self, width, height):
        self.width = width
        self.height = height
        self.area = width * height


r = Rectangle(3, 4)
r.width = 10
print(r.area)
props.task: Make area a property so the program prints 40.

check.question: Why change an account through a deposit() method instead of letting code assign to acct._balance directly?
choices: Attributes can't be changed from outside a class
The method can enforce rules, such as rejecting negative amounts, in one place
Methods run faster than attribute assignment
Python requires every attribute to have a setter method
check.explanation: Python lets you assign any attribute, so rules only hold if changes go through code that checks them. A method centralizes the check, so every caller gets the same protection.

sections.title: Inheritance and super()
sections.key: A subclass inherits its parent's methods and can override them; Python looks methods up from the object's own class upward, and `super()` runs the parent's version.
sections.body:
Admins can do everything users can, plus a few extra things. Copying the User class means every fix is made twice. **Inheritance** lets Admin reuse User's code and change only what differs.

`class Dog(Animal):` makes Dog a **subclass** of Animal, the **superclass**. Dog gets every Animal method and can add new ones, or **override** one by defining a method with the same name.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

If a subclass defines `__init__`, the parent's no longer runs on its own: call `super().__init__(...)`, usually first. Any override can call `super().speak()` to extend the parent's version instead of replacing it.

`isinstance(d, Animal)` is True for a Dog, but `type(d) == Animal` is False; prefer `isinstance`. Inherit only for true **is-a** relationships (a Square is a Shape; a Car is not an Engine), and keep hierarchies shallow.

visual.title: Where Python looks for d.speak
visual.arrowLabel: Searched top down; the first match wins
visual.caption: `d.intro()` is found on Animal, but its `self.speak()` searches from Dog again, so it says Woof.

sections.pitfall: Defining `__init__` in a subclass and forgetting `super().__init__(...)`. The parent's attributes are never set, and the error shows up later as an AttributeError.

activity.title: Extend a parent class
activity.prompt: Give Manager an __init__(self, name, salary, bonus) that calls super().__init__(name, salary) and stores the bonus. Then override annual_pay to return super().annual_pay() plus the bonus, so the parent's formula is reused, not copied.

props.task: Make the program print exactly: Ana 63000

check.question: What does super().__init__(name) do inside Dog.__init__?
choices: Creates a separate Animal object and stores it on the dog
Replaces Dog's __init__ with Animal's for future calls
Runs Animal's __init__ on this same Dog object, so self.name is set
check.explanation: super() gives access to the parent's methods for the current object, so Animal's setup runs on the same self and no second object is created. The inheritance itself comes from writing class Dog(Animal).

sections.title: Polymorphism and duck typing
sections.key: Polymorphism lets one call, like `shape.area()`, run different code for each class; with duck typing, any object that has the method works, shared parent or not.
sections.body:
A drawing app needs the total area of its shapes. Without polymorphism you write "if circle do this, elif rectangle do that" and edit the chain for every new shape. With it, each shape computes its own area and the loop just calls `shape.area()`.

**Polymorphism** means one interface, many implementations. The calling code depends only on the method name, so adding a Triangle needs no change to the loop.

[[visual]]

Python does not even need a shared parent. **Duck typing**: if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck. `thing.sound()` only checks, at that moment, that this object has a `sound` method, which is why `len()` works on any object with `__len__`.

Document what a function expects ("anything with a `value()` method"), and prefer calling methods to checking types.

visual.title: Making subclasses supply a method
columns: If a class forgets the method
rows: Calling it raises NotImplementedError: loud, at call time
Python refuses to create an instance at all
AttributeError when the method is called

sections.pitfall: Long `if isinstance(...)` chains that pick behavior by type. Move the behavior into a method on each class and just call it.

activity.title: Add a new shape
activity.prompt: Run it: Triangle inherits Shape's area(), which raises NotImplementedError. Give Triangle its own area() (half of base times height). Notice that the loop at the bottom needs no change at all.

props.task: Make the loop print three lines: Rect 6, then Triangle 10.0, then Rect 1.

check.question: What is duck typing?
choices: Every class must inherit from a common base class before it can be used
Objects are converted to strings before their methods are called
Python decides whether an object works by checking for the needed method when it's used, not by its class
Methods with the same name in different classes are merged
check.explanation: Python looks up the method on the object at call time, so any object with the right method works, whatever its class or parents.

sections.title: Dunder methods: making objects feel built in
sections.key: Dunder methods let your objects work with built-in syntax: `__str__` for print, `__repr__` for debugging, `__eq__` for `==` and `__lt__` for sorting.
sections.body:
Print a new object and you get `<__main__.Point object at 0x7f3a...>`; compare two identical points with `==` and you get False. **Dunder methods** (double underscore, or magic methods) fix that: Python calls them when you use built-in syntax on your objects.

[[visual]]

When `__eq__` gets an object it cannot compare, it should `return NotImplemented` (a special value, not the exception), so Python can try the other side or fall back to False.

Defining `__eq__` makes instances unhashable unless you also define `__hash__`, so they cannot go in a set or be dict keys. For simple data classes, `@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` for you.

Call dunders through the syntax (`len(x)`, not `x.__len__()`), and do not invent new dunder names.

rows: The object starts with no attributes
Return a string (printing inside it makes print raise TypeError)
Falls back to `__repr__`, so define `__repr__` first
The REPL, `repr(p)`, and `p` inside a list or dict
Look like code that recreates it: `Point(1, 2)`
`==` compares identity, so separate objects are never equal

sections.pitfall: Printing inside `__str__` instead of returning a string. print() then receives None and raises TypeError: __str__ returned non-string.

activity.title: Make Money print and compare
activity.prompt: Add __str__ returning the amount in dollars with two decimals (cents / 100 with :.2f), and __eq__ comparing cents. Run before and after each method to see what Python does by default.

props.code:
class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents):
        self.cents = cents


a = Money(250)
b = Money(250)
print(a)
print(a == b)
props.task: Make the program print $2.50 and then True.

check.question: Which dunder method controls what print(obj) displays?
check.explanation: print() calls str() on the object, and str() calls __str__ (falling back to __repr__). __init__ sets the object up, __eq__ is used by ==, and __len__ by len().

sections.title: Composition, and a small worked design
sections.key: Model has-a relationships with composition, storing other objects as attributes and calling their methods; save inheritance for true is-a relationships.
sections.body:
Inheritance answers "is a kind of". Most real relationships are "has a": a car has an engine, an order has line items. **Composition** stores other objects as attributes and calls their methods, which is called **delegation**.

It is usually more flexible: swap parts (an electric engine for a gas one), test each part alone, combine small classes freely. Inheritance couples a subclass to its parent's internals. "Favor composition over inheritance" means inherit only when is-a is real.

[[visual]]

[[visual 2]]

No class reaches into another's internals: the library calls `book.check_out()` and `member.borrow(book)` instead of flipping flags itself. Reviewers look for exactly that in a take-home project.

sections.pitfall: Inheriting just to reuse a few methods, such as `class Library(list)`. You get dozens of list methods that make no sense for a library; hold a list or dict as an attribute instead.

activity.title: Extend the library design
activity.prompt: Add a give_back(book) method to Member, a check_in() method to Book, and a return_book(name, title) method to Library that uses both. Keep each change inside the class that owns the data.

props.task: Implement return_book so the program prints [Book('Emma')] and then False.

check.question: A Library keeps a collection of Book objects. Which design fits best?
choices: Library stores a list or dict of Book objects in an attribute
Library and Book merge into one class with a type flag
check.explanation: A library has books; it isn't a kind of book. That has-a relationship calls for composition, such as self.books = {}. Inheriting from Book would give Library methods like check_out, which make no sense for a library.

keyTerms.definition: A blueprint that defines the attributes and methods its objects will have.
One object built from a class, with its own attribute values.
The first parameter of an instance method: the object the method was called on.
The initializer Python calls on a new object to set its starting attributes.
A value assigned in the class body and shared by every instance.
Keeping an object's state behind methods so its rules always hold.
A method decorated with @property and read like an attribute; read-only unless it has a setter.
A subclass reusing and extending a parent class's code; models is-a relationships.
Different classes responding to the same method call in their own way.
Using any object that has the needed methods, regardless of its class.
A method like __str__ or __eq__ that Python calls for built-in syntax.
Building objects from other objects held as attributes; models has-a relationships.

summary: A class bundles data (attributes) with behavior (methods); each instance has its own values.
__init__ sets up a new object, and self is the instance a method was called on.
Class attributes are shared by every instance, so create per-object lists in __init__.
Protect rules with methods that validate and raise, and with read-only properties.
Subclasses override methods and call super(); polymorphism lets one call work across classes.
Dunder methods make objects work with print, == and sorted; favor composition for has-a.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend who knows functions but not classes what self is, why acct.deposit(50) changes only that one account, and when you would use inheritance versus composition.

questions.question: Calling g.hello() raises TypeError. Why?
choices: hello is missing the self parameter, so it can't accept the instance Python passes in
Methods must be called on the class, as Greeter.hello()
A class needs an __init__ method before its methods can be called
return can't be used inside a class
questions.explanation: g.hello() really calls Greeter.hello(g), so the method receives one argument, but it was defined to take none: TypeError, takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given. Classes don't need an __init__. The fix is def hello(self).

questions.question: Complete __init__ so each book stores its own title.
questions.code:
class Book:
    def __init__(self, title, pages):
        _____ = title
        self.pages = pages

a = Book("Dune", 412)
b = Book("Emma", 474)
print(a.title, b.title)   # should print Dune Emma
questions.explanation: self.title = title stores the value on this instance. A bare title = title only reassigns a local variable that disappears when __init__ ends. Book.title would set one class attribute shared by every book, so this code would print Emma Emma. this isn't defined in Python.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The list starts with one item. Each add() call appends to self.items on the same instance, so after cup and key it holds 3 items, and the second call returns 3.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
class Lamp:
    def __init__(self):
        self.on = False

    def toggle(self):
        self.on = not self.on

a = Lamp()
b = Lamp()
a.toggle()
a.toggle()
b.toggle()
print(a.on, b.on)
questions.explanation: Each Lamp has its own self.on. a toggles twice, ending back at False, and b toggles once, ending at True. Toggling a never affects b.
questions.concept: each instance has its own state

questions.question: red.join("Ana") also adds Ana to the blue team. Why?
choices: append() copies the person into every list in the program
self.members creates a new list on every call
red and blue are the same object because they come from one class
members is a class attribute, so every team shares one list; create self.members = [] in __init__
questions.explanation: The list is created once, in the class body, and every instance reaches that same list through self.members. append() changes the shared list instead of creating an instance attribute. Each team needs its own list made in __init__.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
class Car:
    wheels = 4

c = Car()
c.wheels = 3
Car.wheels = 6
d = Car()
print(c.wheels + d.wheels)
questions.explanation: c.wheels = 3 creates an instance attribute on c, which hides the class value. Car.wheels = 6 changes the class attribute, which d sees because d has no wheels of its own. 3 + 6 = 9.

questions.question: Complete the line so User.count tracks how many users have been created.
questions.code:
class User:
    count = 0

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        _____ += 1

User("ana")
User("ben")
print(User.count)   # should print 2
questions.explanation: User.count += 1 updates the shared class attribute. self.count += 1 reads the class value 0 but writes a new instance attribute, so User.count stays 0. A bare count += 1 raises UnboundLocalError, because count is not a local variable.

questions.question: Why does print(b.wheels) raise AttributeError?
choices: Bike must also define wheels as a class attribute
Bike.__init__ replaces Vehicle.__init__ and never calls it, so wheels is never set; call super().__init__(2)
Subclasses can't access attributes defined in the parent
Bike must inherit from object as well as Vehicle
questions.explanation: Defining __init__ in Bike overrides the parent's version, so Vehicle.__init__ never runs and self.wheels is never assigned. Subclasses can use parent attributes once they exist. Add super().__init__(2) at the start of Bike.__init__.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: hello() is inherited from A, but self is a B instance, so self.who() finds B's override and returns "B". Method lookup starts from the object's own class at the moment of the call.
questions.concept: overridden methods are found through self

questions.question: Complete the line so Manager runs Employee's setup before adding reports.
questions.explanation: super().__init__(name, salary) runs the parent's setup on this same object. self.__init__ would call Manager's own __init__ again with too few arguments, Employee() tries to build a separate object without arguments, and super without parentheses is the built-in type, not a link to the parent.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Coin doesn't define __eq__, so == falls back to identity and asks whether both sides are the same object. They are two separate objects, so the result is False even though the values match. Define __eq__ to compare values.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Putting an object inside an f-string calls its __str__, just like print() does. __str__ returns "21C", so the full text is Now: 21C. Without __str__ you would see something like <__main__.Temp object at 0x...>.

questions.question: Duck and Robot share no parent class apart from object. Why does this loop still work?
choices: Python creates a hidden common parent class for them
Both classes inherit sound() from object
Python only needs each object to have a sound() method at the moment it is called
The loop converts each item to a string first
questions.explanation: Python looks up the method on each object when the call runs, so any object with a sound() method works. This is duck typing. object has no sound() method, and nothing is generated behind the scenes.

questions.question: This prints Card Q and then crashes. Why?
choices: __str__ prints instead of returning, so it returns None and print() raises TypeError
rank must be an int for __str__ to work
questions.explanation: print(card) calls __str__ and expects a string back. This __str__ prints Card Q itself and returns None, so Python raises TypeError: __str__ returned non-string. Replace print(...) with return ... inside __str__.

questions.question: What happens when this runs?
choices: SyntaxError, because private attributes can't be read
AttributeError, because Python stores the attribute as _Safe__code
questions.explanation: Two leading underscores trigger name mangling inside the class body, so the attribute is stored as _Safe__code and s.__code doesn't exist outside the class. It isn't true privacy: s._Safe__code still works.

questions.question: Which pair is best modeled with composition rather than inheritance?
questions.explanation: A car has an engine; it isn't a kind of engine, so Car should hold an Engine attribute. The other pairs are is-a relationships: a dog is an animal, a savings account is an account, and a square is a shape.

questions.question: When should you choose composition over inheritance?
questions.answer: Use inheritance when the subclass truly is a kind of the parent and can be used anywhere the parent is expected. Use composition for has-a relationships, or when you only need part of another class's behavior: hold the other object as an attribute and call its methods.
questions.explanation: Composition keeps classes loosely coupled, so you can swap one part, such as a different Engine, without changing a class hierarchy.

questions.question: What is the relationship between a class and an instance?
choices: A class is a blueprint, and an instance is one object built from it with its own attribute values
A class is a running copy of an instance
An instance is a function defined inside a class
They are two names for the same thing
questions.explanation: The class defines which attributes and methods objects will have. Each call like Player("Ana") builds a separate instance whose attribute values are its own, while the methods are shared through the class.

questions.question: Match each term to an example from a Player class.
questions.explanation: The class is the blueprint, an instance is one object made from it, an attribute is data stored on the object, and a method is a function defined in the class and called on an object.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: increment returns self, the same object, so the second call runs on c too. 10 + 1 = 11, then 11 + 5 = 16. Returning self is what makes method chaining work.

questions.question: Circle(2).area() raises NameError: name 'r' is not defined. Why?
choices: area needs its own r parameter
Inside area, the radius must be read as self.r; a bare r is looked up as a local or global name
Attributes set in __init__ are deleted when __init__ ends
questions.explanation: The parameter r only existed during __init__. The value lives on the object as self.r, so methods must read it through self. Attributes stay on the object for its whole life.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: from_string is a class method, so cls is Date. It splits the text into "2024", "03" and "09", converts them to ints and calls Date(2024, 3, 9). month + day is 3 + 9 = 12.

questions.question: What happens on the last line?
choices: AttributeError, because balance is a property with no setter
SyntaxError, because properties can't appear on the left of =
questions.explanation: A property without a setter is read-only, so assigning to it raises AttributeError. The balance can only change through methods you write, which is the point. It isn't a syntax error, because the check happens when the line runs.

questions.question: Complete the method so withdrawing too much stops with an error.
questions.explanation: raise stops the method and sends the exception to the caller. return ValueError(...) would hand back an error object without stopping anything, throw is JavaScript and Java syntax, and except only appears in try blocks.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: isinstance respects inheritance, and a Square is a Shape, so it is True. type(s) is exactly Square, so comparing it with Shape gives False. That's why isinstance is usually the better check.

questions.question: d is a Dog, and Dog inherits from Animal. Put the places Python checks for d.speak in order.
items: object, the root of every class
questions.explanation: Lookup starts with the object, then walks up its class and the parents. The first match wins, which is how an override in Dog hides Animal's version. If nothing matches, Python raises AttributeError.

questions.question: This prints 3 and then raises NotImplementedError. Why?
choices: Circle's area overrides Shape's for every subclass
Square never overrides area, so it inherits the base version that raises; add an area method to Square
A for loop can't call methods on objects of different classes
NotImplementedError is raised because Shape has no __init__
questions.explanation: Each class gets its own lookup. Circle has area, but Square falls back to Shape.area, which deliberately raises to flag the missing method. That's the point of the pattern: forgetting an override fails loudly.
questions.concept: base methods that must be overridden

questions.question: Point defines __str__ returning "(1, 2)" but no __repr__. What does print([Point(1, 2)]) show?
questions.explanation: Printing a list uses repr() for each item, and without __repr__ you get the default object description. That's why __repr__ is the one to define if you only define one: str() falls back to it, but repr() doesn't fall back to __str__.

questions.question: Match each dunder method to the code that triggers it.
questions.explanation: Python translates built-in syntax into dunder calls: creating an object calls __init__, print calls __str__, == calls __eq__, len() calls __len__ and < calls __lt__.
